item.title: One or two severe cyclones likely to affect the country
item.description: Fijians are being urged to remain alert and prepared for the upcoming 2026–2027 tropical cyclone season, with one to two severe tropical cyclones likely to affect the country. The Fiji Meteorological Service says two to three tropical cyclones are likely to pass through Fiji’s Exclusive Economic Zone between November this year to April next year, indicating near-normal tropical cyclone activity.
item.content:encoded:
Fijians are being urged to remain alert and prepared for the upcoming 2026–2027 tropical cyclone season, with one to two severe tropical cyclones likely to affect the country.

The Fiji Meteorological Service says two to three tropical cyclones are likely to pass through Fiji’s Exclusive Economic Zone between November this year to April next year, indicating near-normal tropical cyclone activity.

It says one to two severe tropical cyclones, classified as Category 3 to Category 5, are likely to affect Fiji during the season.

The Weather Office says the analysis of past tropical cyclone tracks in similar seasons indicates that all parts of Fiji face an equal risk of being affected, meaning no part of the country should be considered less vulnerable .

The Fiji Meteorological Service also warns that tropical cyclones can occur outside the official season, which runs from 1st November to 30th April, with Fiji having previously experienced cyclones in May and October.

It says tropical disturbances and depressions that do not reach tropical cyclone intensity, as well as low-pressure systems left by decaying cyclones, can still bring widespread rainfall and potential flooding.

The Weather Office warns that flooding could also increase the risk of waterborne disease outbreaks in communities, as experienced during previous post-flooding events.

Members of the public are urged to strengthen their homes, roofs and surrounding structures, clear drains and gutters, and prepare emergency kits containing drinking water, food, essential medicines, torches, batteries and important documents.

Farmers, fishers and tourism operators are also encouraged to review their emergency and business continuity plans, while households should identify evacuation routes and safe places to shelter.

The Fiji Meteorological Service says the public should continue to follow official tropical cyclone alerts, warnings and advisories issued throughout the season to help reduce loss of life and damage to property.

People can access the latest seasonal outlook, forecasts and warnings through the Fiji Meteorological Service website at www.met.gov.fj .

item.title: Human Rights Commission calls for extension of Constitution Bill submissions
item.description: The Fiji Human Rights and Anti-Discrimination Commission is calling on Parliament to extend the 11-day public submission period for the Constitution Amendment Bill 2026, warning that the timeframe limits meaningful public participation in a process that will shape Fiji’s democratic future. Commissioner Alefina Vuki says the public needs adequate time and accessible information to understand the pr
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Human Rights and Anti-Discrimination Commission is calling on Parliament to extend the 11-day public submission period for the Constitution Amendment Bill 2026, warning that the timeframe limits meaningful public participation in a process that will shape Fiji’s democratic future.

Commissioner Alefina Vuki says the public needs adequate time and accessible information to understand the proposed amendments and their implications before providing feedback.

The Special Committee reviewing the Bill issued a notice yesterday, setting October 23rd as the deadline for written submissions.

Vuki says this timeframe leaves less than two working weeks for individuals, communities and organisations to examine the proposed changes and prepare informed submissions.

She says the process is particularly challenging because the public would need to understand both the draft Constitution prepared by the Constitution Review Committee and the revised draft containing substantial changes made by the Government.

Vuki says meaningful consultation requires more than publishing a Bill and inviting submissions, as people must understand what is being proposed, why the changes are being sought and how they could affect them.

She says Fiji’s geographical circumstances also present challenges, with people in rural communities, remote villages and maritime islands facing varying levels of access to information, transport and internet connectivity.

She says they are also calling for measures to ensure vulnerable and marginalised groups, including people with disabilities, older persons, women, young people and people living in poverty, can participate in the consultation process.

Vuki says this requires accessible information, translations into relevant languages, reasonable accommodation and proactive community engagement.

The Commission has also raised concerns about the proposed national referendum, saying voters need sufficient time and impartial information to understand the process, the choices they will be asked to make and the consequences of their decisions.

She says comprehensive civic education is necessary to ensure the referendum is an informed exercise rather than simply a voting process.

They also note that Fiji, as a State Party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, has obligations under Article 25 to protect citizens’ rights and opportunities to participate in public affairs without unreasonable restrictions.

They argue that limiting submissions to 11 days while moving towards a proposed referendum on December 9th this year risks undermining that right.
